lesson.title: Separable Verbs
lesson.subtitle: opbellen, meebrengen, aankomen — the prefix walks to the end

hook.title: The Prefix Walks to the End
hook.content: Dutch separable verbs are two halves of one idea. Opbellen becomes ik bel je op; meebrengen becomes ik breng het mee; aankomen becomes hij komt aan. The prefix is not a preposition — it is the verb's other half.

pattern.title: Split the verb, park the prefix
pattern.content: In a main clause the finite part takes second place and the prefix goes to the end. Ik bel je op, ik breng het mee, hij komt morgen aan. The two halves frame the sentence like a bracket.
pattern.linguist_note: Separable prefixes are stressed particles that behave like the second half of a compound verb; Dutch main-clause order separates them.
pattern.trap_note: Do not leave the prefix attached in a main clause: ik opbel je is wrong. The prefix belongs at the end.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Separable Verbs):
exercises.target_answer: opbellen, meebrengen, aankomen, bellen, brengen, komen
exercises.meaning: to call (phone), to bring along, to arrive, to call, phone, to bring, to come
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Separable Verbs": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Ik bel je op.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Separable Verbs”.

cues: The pattern: Split the verb, park the prefix
It means: I bring it along.
exercises.explanation: “Ik breng het mee.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Split the verb, park the prefix.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not leave the prefix attached in a main clause: ik opbel je is wrong. The prefix belongs at the end.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Hij komt morgen aan.” is word-for-word “He comes tomorrow at.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Split the verb, park the prefix.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “Wij bellen haar op.” reuses only material taught in “Separable Verbs” — Split the verb, park the prefix.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Wij bellen haar op.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Split the verb, park the prefix.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I bring the book along.”
twist.explanation: The finite breng is second; mee closes the sentence.

summary.outcome: Split separable verbs in main clauses and park the prefix at the end.
summary.takeaway: A separable verb is a bracket: one meaning, two halves, the rest of the sentence inside.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Separable Verb Gym.

opbellen.etymology_derivation: Separable: op + bellen. A bell was the old way to call someone.

bellen.etymology_derivation: From the bell used to call; Dutch turned it into the everyday phone verb.

brengen.etymology_derivation: English bring and Dutch brengen are the same verb.

komen.etymology_derivation: English come and Dutch komen are the same verb; the vowel differs.
